verdict: This is in the index as a reality check. You roll it on its side, the clumps fall into a tray, you pull the tray. It costs $45, uses no power, has nothing to break and no consumables. It is not automatic and it has no odor system beyond a hood — but for a single cat on a tight budget, it removes the daily scooping for about the price of two months of ScoopFree trays.
pros: No motor, no firmware, nothing to fail
Nothing can pinch or trap a cat
cons: Entirely manual — you still handle it daily
No odor control beyond the hood
No app, alerts or weight data

sections.setup: Five minutes. Clip the two halves together, add clumping litter, done. No power, no app, no pairing.
sections.app: There is no app, and no electronics of any kind. That is the point.
sections.odorControl: A hood and nothing else. It is the worst odor result here by a wide margin, and it depends entirely on you emptying the tray daily and on the room having ventilation.
sections.cleaning: You roll the box onto its side and back; clumps fall through a grate into a pull-out tray. It works, but it misses material against the seams and needs a full wash more often than any powered box.
sections.safety: Nothing can pinch, trap or start unexpectedly, because nothing moves without you. On pure risk it is the safest object in this index, which is why it scores 9.6 — a fair score that should not be read as a recommendation over a good powered box.
sections.consumables: None. No bags, no filters, no trays, no subscription.
sections.longTermCost: Around $45 once and nothing thereafter. Over five years it costs less than a single year of ScoopFree trays. What you spend instead is your own time, every day.
